title: Basic Control
summary: Keep your body relaxed yet fairly upright so your arms are free to steer instead of propping you up.
Sit at a distance where your arms are slightly bent when you hold the handlebars, so you can turn them without stretching.
Grip the handlegrips firmly and begin with your wrists flat to avoid adding too much throttle by accident.
Set the handlebars so your hands are level with or lower than your elbows, press your knees against the tank, and keep your feet on the footpegs near the controls with toes not pointing down.
The recommended turning sequence is Slow, Look, Lean, Roll. Get your speed down before the turn, closing the throttle and using both brakes if needed.
To lean, press the handgrip on the side you want to go: press left to go left, press right to go right; faster or tighter turns need more lean.

Turn your head (not your shoulders) to look through the turn, keeping your eyes level with the horizon. Once in the turn, roll on the throttle to hold a steady speed or speed up gradually rather than slowing down.
In normal turns rider and motorcycle lean together; in slow, tight turns only the motorcycle leans while the body stays upright.

The front brake can supply at least three-quarters of the stopping power. Use both brakes together whenever you slow down or stop, squeezing the front lever and pressing the rear pedal, since grabbing or jamming them can lock the brakes and cost you control.
With the right technique you can use the front brake while leaned in a turn, but leaning uses up some traction, leaving less for stopping, so too much brake can cause a skid.

Downshift through every gear as you slow, but only when you are going slowly enough for the lower gear, since too fast can make the bike lurch and the rear wheel skid; going downhill or shifting into first, you may need to brake before you can shift safely. Stay in first while stopped. Shift before a turn when you can, and mid-turn only if you can do it smoothly.

On a hill, hold the bike with the front brake while you start the engine and select first, then switch to the foot brake so your right hand can work the throttle. Open the throttle slightly, ease the clutch out gradually, and let go of the foot brake when the engine starts to slow, which means it is taking hold.

questions.q: What is the proper body posture for controlling a motorcycle?
options: Leaning far forward with your weight on the handlebars
Tense and rigid so you stay firmly planted
Relaxed but fairly erect
Slouched back so your arms are fully extended
questions.explanation: A relaxed, fairly upright posture lets your arms steer the motorcycle rather than support your body.

questions.q: How close to the handlebars should you sit?
options: Close enough that your arms are slightly bent when holding the grips
Far enough back that your arms are fully straight and locked at the elbows
So close that your elbows touch your knees
As far back on the seat as possible, to keep the motorcycle more stable
questions.explanation: Slightly bent arms let you turn the handlebars without stretching to reach them.

questions.q: Why should you start with your wrists flat when holding the handlegrips?
options: It makes the turn signals easier to reach
It reduces vibration from the engine
It lets you rest your palms on top of the grips
It helps prevent accidentally applying too much throttle
questions.explanation: Flat wrists keep you from rolling on excess throttle by mistake, especially when you reach for the brake suddenly.

questions.q: How should the handlebars be adjusted?
options: So your hands are above your shoulders
So your hands are even with or below your elbows
So your arms are fully straight
So your hands are level with or higher than your chin
questions.explanation: The manual says to position the bars so your hands sit level with or lower than your elbows.

questions.q: What should you do with your knees while riding?
options: Hold them out away from the tank for balance
Keep them loose so you can shift your weight
Hold them firmly against the gas tank
Rest them on the engine guards
questions.explanation: Pressing your knees against the tank helps you stay balanced as the motorcycle turns.

questions.q: Which is correct foot positioning while riding?
options: Feet firmly on the footpegs, near the controls, toes not pointed down
Toes pointed downward so they can touch the ground quickly when needed
Feet dragging lightly along the ground to help balance in slow turns
Feet off the pegs and away from the controls until needed
questions.explanation: Keep both feet planted on the pegs, near the controls; a dragged foot or a downward-pointing toe can catch on the road and hurt you or cost you control. The manual's one exception is snow or ice you cannot avoid, where you creep across with your feet skimming the surface.

questions.q: What are the four recommended steps for better control in a turn, in order?
options: Look, Slow, Roll, Lean
Lean, Look, Slow, Roll
Roll, Lean, Look, Slow
Slow, Look, Lean, Roll
questions.explanation: The manual's turning sequence is Slow, Look, Lean, Roll. Many rider courses, including the MSF's, call the third step Press; the manual's word is Lean.

questions.q: When looking through a turn, you should:
options: Look down at the road just in front of your front tire until the turn ends
Turn just your head, not your shoulders, and keep your eyes level with the horizon
Turn your shoulders along with your head, and tilt your head to match the lean
Keep your head still and your eyes fixed straight ahead until the turn is complete
questions.explanation: Look where you want to go by turning your head only, keeping your eyes level with the horizon.

questions.q: To make the motorcycle lean and go left, you should:
options: Press on the right handgrip
Pull back on the left handgrip
Press on the left handgrip
Shift your weight to the right footpeg
questions.explanation: Pressing the handgrip on the side of the turn leans the bike that way: press left, lean left, go left.

questions.q: What should you do with the throttle while riding through a turn?
options: Roll on the throttle to maintain steady speed or accelerate gradually
Close the throttle completely and coast
Close the throttle and apply the rear brake
Rapidly open and close the throttle to keep the bike balanced
questions.explanation: The 'Roll' step means keeping a steady speed or gradually accelerating; slowing down in the turn should be avoided.

questions.q: In a slow, tight turn, how should you position your body?
options: Lean your body farther than the motorcycle
Keep the motorcycle upright and lean only your body into the turn
Lean together with the motorcycle at the same angle
Keep your body upright and lean only the motorcycle
questions.explanation: In slow, tight turns only the motorcycle leans; in normal turns rider and bike lean together.

questions.q: How much of a motorcycle's total stopping power can the front brake provide?
options: About one-quarter
About one-half
At least three-quarters
Almost none; the rear brake does most of the work
questions.explanation: The manual says the front brake is the stronger of the two and can supply three-quarters or more of your total stopping power.

questions.q: When should you use both the front and rear brakes?
options: Every time you slow down or stop
Only during emergency stops
Only when riding at highway speeds
Only when carrying a passenger
questions.explanation: Using both brakes even for normal stops builds the skill to use them correctly in an emergency.

questions.q: What is the correct timing for applying the front and rear brakes?
options: Apply the rear brake first, then the front
Apply the front brake only after the rear wheel begins to slow
Use only the rear brake for most stops
Apply both brakes at the same time
questions.explanation: Apply both brakes at once. The common belief that the rear brake should go first is wrong: the sooner the front brake goes on, the sooner it starts slowing you.

questions.q: What can happen if you grab the front brake or jam down on the rear brake?
options: The engine may stall but braking improves
The brakes can lock, causing control problems
The motorcycle will automatically straighten up
Nothing, as long as you are traveling in a straight line
questions.explanation: Squeeze the front and press the rear; abrupt application can lock the brakes and lead to loss of control.

questions.q: Which statement about braking while the motorcycle is leaned in a turn is correct?
options: The front brake must never be used in a turn, because even a light touch of it will cause a skid
Leaning increases the traction available, so you can brake harder than when upright
The front brake can be used with proper technique, but less traction is available for stopping
Hard braking is safe while leaned, as long as you use only the rear brake
questions.explanation: Leaning uses some of your traction for cornering, so less is left for stopping and too much braking with either brake can cause a skid. The front brake can still be used in a turn if your technique is right.

questions.q: When slowing down or stopping, how should you handle the gears?
options: Shift down through all the gears and remain in first while stopped
Shift straight into neutral and coast, staying in neutral while stopped
Stay in your current gear, then shift to neutral once you have stopped
Skip to second gear and hold the clutch in
questions.explanation: Downshift through every gear and stay in first at a stop so you can move quickly if needed.

questions.q: What may happen if you shift into a lower gear while traveling too fast?
options: The front wheel may lift off the ground
The motorcycle may lurch and the rear wheel may skid
The front brake may lock and the front tire may skid
The engine will automatically shift back up
questions.explanation: Downshifting at too high a speed can make the bike lurch and the rear wheel skid, so make sure you are slow enough first. The manual links a lifting front wheel to letting the clutch out too fast on a hill start, not to downshifting.

questions.q: What is the recommended practice for shifting gears in relation to a turn?
options: Upshift in the middle of every turn to keep speed steady
Downshift partway through the turn for more control
Shift in the turn whenever you like, since it does not affect traction
Change gears before entering the turn
questions.explanation: The manual recommends changing gears before you enter a turn. Shift in a turn only when you have to and only if you can do it smoothly, because an abrupt change in power at the rear wheel can make it lock or spin and cause a skid.

questions.q: When starting on a hill, after using the front brake to hold the motorcycle while you start the engine and shift into first, what should you do next?
options: Release both brakes together and let the clutch out quickly to get moving
Keep squeezing the front brake lever while you open the throttle with the same hand
Switch to the foot brake to hold the bike so your right hand can operate the throttle
Let the motorcycle roll back slightly so that it builds momentum before you pull away
questions.explanation: Moving to the foot brake frees your right hand for the throttle; release the foot brake once the engine begins to slow and take hold.
